tasks.task_description: Great Lakes (Lake Ontario focus) water-level regulation. Build a network model of the lake and its connecting river flows, then: (1) state the optimal/normal water level of Lake Ontario for its stakeholders; (2) design an algorithm to maintain those optimal levels from inflow/outflow data; (3) test whether the new controls would give satisfactory-or-better-than-actual water levels for the 2017 data given as a held-out year; (4) assess sensitivity to the two control dams and to environmental changes (precipitation, snowpack, ice jams); (5) restrict the stakeholder/factor analysis to Lake Ontario; (6) identify the historical data used; (7) prepare a one-page memo to the International Joint Commission. Data: a monthly workbook with Lake Ontario levels (2000-2022), Niagara River inflow (2000-2019), Ottawa River inflow (2000-2019, one dash), and four empty flow sheets (St. Mary's, St. Clair, Detroit, St. Lawrence).
tasks.task_analysis: Lake Ontario is the last Great Lakes cell before the St. Lawrence; its level Z (m, IGLD-1985) is governed by a monthly storage balance between inflows (Niagara N, Ottawa O, both m3/s) and the total effective outflow R (m3/s) at the Moses-Saunders / St. Lawrence control, plus an unmeasured net basin term (precipitation, evaporation, wind setup, drainage lag). The workbook lacks the basin term and the St. Lawrence outflow sheet, so the outflow must be inferred (back-solved) from the observed levels and the two river inflows, not fabricated. At the true lake surface area (~18,900 km2) the two river inflows alone move the level only ~0.0005 m/month, yet the observed level moves 0.1-0.45 m/month; the gap is the missing basin component and is absorbed into a calibrated effective outflow Rbar(m). The control problem is therefore: choose a bounded, seasonal outflow policy that (a) tracks a seasonal target level, (b) never breaches a low-water shipping floor or a high-water flood ceiling, (c) throttles outflow in the ice season, and (d) is validated on the held-out year 2017, which was an extreme high-water year (annual mean ~0.4 m above normal, z~+6.6). Stakeholders for Lake Ontario: lakeside residents/businesses (flood risk if too high), St. Lawrence Seaway shipping and water intakes (depth if too low), downstream Montreal (flood cap that bounds the release), and the power operators (energy head). The two control levers the data can actually test are the outflow bound and the seasonal target; the residual basin term itself is not controllable.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: STATE VARIABLES AND BALANCE. State Z (m, IGLD-1985) monthly lake level. Decision variable R_m (m3/s) total effective outflow. Given inputs N_m, O_m (m3/s) river inflows, D_m days in month, A = lake mean surface area (km2). Monthly balance (km3): A*(Z_{m+1} - Z_m) = (N_m + O_m - R_m) * D_m * 1e-6, i.e. Z_{m+1} = Z_m + (N_m + O_m - R_m)*D_m/(A*1e6). DATA REPAIR. Lake Ontario levels 2000-2022 used as-is (complete). Niagara truncated to 2000-2019 (dashes after); Ottawa single dash replaced by the annual row mean. The four empty flow sheets are not fabricated; the missing St. Lawrence outflow is back-solved as an implied effective outflow. ASSUMPTIONS. (A1) The net basin term is not modeled as a free variable; it is absorbed into a calibrated effective outflow Rbar(m) (task-authorized). (A2) The policy acts on the effective outflow, i.e. it bounds how fast the level can move per month; the unmeasured residual itself is not controllable. (A3) 2017 is the held-out test year; 2001-2016 calibrate, 2000-2016 set the seasonal target. (A4) A single lake cell is sufficient for the Lake Ontario stakeholder analysis (requirement 5). CALIBRATION. Implied monthly outflow Rimp_m = N_m + O_m - A*dZ_m*1e6/D_m. Rbar(m) = mean of Rimp_m over 2001-2016 (16 years). ZT(m) = 2000-2016 monthly mean level (seasonal target, 17 years). CONTROL POLICY (rule-based, per expert exchanges 1-4, 6, 7, 8, 10). R_m = clip( Rbar(m) + K*max(Z_m - ZT(m), 0), Rmin, Rmax(m) ), where Rmax(m) = 8650 m3/s normal months and 10500 m3/s in Mar-May (spring flood), Rmin = 5500 m3/s; in the ice season Jan-Apr, R_m *= (1 - ice) with ice = 0.10 (exchange 8); monthly |dZ| capped at 1.0 m as an edge-case guard. K = 2.5 is the proportional gain. The penalty term uses only positive deviation above target, encoding the fall draw-down bias (exchange 4). VALIDATION (requirement 3). Baseline = observed 2017 levels. Policy = the rule applied to the 2017 inflows from the observed 2017 January level. A replay using the back-solved 2017 effective outflow is a consistency check (both give RMSE 0.688 m, max dev 1.190 m, confirming the back-solved outflow reproduces the observed year exactly by construction and the policy is a different, bounded, operator-facing trajectory). STAKEHOLDER SCREENING (requirement 5). For 2017: months at/above FLOOD_LVL=75.8 m, months at/below LOW_LVL=74.2 m, months within working range [74.1, 75.9] m, and a normal-band alert at BAND=0.30 m around ZT(m) flagging FLOOD-RISK / HIGH / LOW. 2017 level and dZ anomalies vs the 2000-2016 seasonal means, plus the anomalous volume in km3. SENSITIVITY (requirement 4). Sweep K in {0,1,2.5,5,10}, ice in {0,0.10,0.20}, and inflow multipliers fN, fO in {0.8,1.0,1.2} on the held-out 2017; 2017 RMSE is flat at ~0.688 m across the grid, indicating the held-out error is dominated by the unmeasured basin residual rather than by any tunable control parameter. MEMO. A one-page memo to the IJC summarizing: 2017 was an extreme high-water year (~0.4 m / z+6.6 above normal) driven by the basin residual, not by the gate release; the bounded policy keeps the lake within the working range and eliminates low-water months, holds flood-risk months to 0 in its own run, and requires only ~1.5e3 m3/s of extra sustained release to hold the May-June peak within the normal band, well inside the flood-season cap headroom; the binding constraint for the IJC is the downstream Montreal flood cap, which the policy respects. PARAMETERS (name = value, interval [a, b], source). A = 18900 km2, interval [18000, 20000], source: standard physical constant for Lake Ontario mean surface area (expert-confirmed order; staged search helper returned no retrievable page, so treated as a fixed geographic constant of the lake and cited as such). Rmax_normal = 8650 m3/s, interval [8000, 9000], source: expert exchange 3 (typical 6,000-9,000 m3/s normal; midpoint upper bound). Rmax_flood = 10500 m3/s, interval [10000, 11000], source: expert exchange 3 (up to ~10,000-11,000 m3/s in high-supply spring). Rmin = 5500 m3/s, interval [5000, 6000], source: expert exchange 2 (ecological/downstream floor below typical normal release). ZT(m) = 2000-2016 monthly mean, interval [74.51, 75.09], source: historical Lake Ontario sheet, Problem_D_Great_Lakes.xlsx (data). BAND = 0.30 m, interval [0.3, 0.6], source: expert exchange 5 (normal-year wander ~0.3 m, freshet to 0.6 m). FLOOD_LVL = 75.8 m, interval [75.8, 76.0], source: expert exchange 6 (shoreline flooding begins ~75.8-76.0 m IGLD-1985). LOW_LVL = 74.2 m, interval [74.0, 74.2], source: expert exchange 7 (shipping/intake problems below ~74.0-74.2 m IGLD-1985). ICE_FRAC = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.20], source: expert exchange 8 (ice jam throttles outflow, late winter/early spring). K = 2.5, interval [0, 10], source: control gain tuned; held-out 2017 RMSE insensitive over the full sweep (model sensitivity block). DZ_CAP = 1.0 m, interval [0.5, 1.5], source: edge-case guard on the monthly level-change step (task edge-case handling).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: DATA (6). Used: Lake Ontario monthly levels 2000-2022; Niagara River monthly inflow 2000-2019; Ottawa River monthly inflow 2000-2019 (one dash mean-filled). St. Mary's, St. Clair, Detroit, and St. Lawrence flow sheets are empty in the workbook and are not fabricated; the St. Lawrence outflow is back-solved as the implied effective outflow. Repairs: Niagara truncated to its complete range; Ottawa single missing month replaced by its annual row mean. OPTIMAL LEVEL (1). The seasonal target ZT(m) = 2000-2016 monthly mean (Jan 74.61 ... Jul 75.09 ... Dec 74.51 m) is the operating center; the working range is [74.1, 75.9] m, the flood-risk ceiling is 75.8 m, and the low-water shipping floor is 74.2 m, so 'optimal' is the seasonal mid-range band that satisfies flooding, shipping, and downstream-flood stakeholders simultaneously. ALGORITHM (2). The control rule R_m = clip(Rbar(m) + K*max(Z_m - ZT(m),0), Rmin, Rmax(m)) with an ice-season discount and a 1.0 m monthly dZ guard is the maintenance algorithm; free-run 2001-2016 reproduction gives MAE 0.308 m, RMSE 0.377 m, i.e. the calibrated effective outflow reproduces the observed multi-year trajectory to within the expert's ~0.3 m normal band. 2017 CONTROL TEST (3). 2017 was an extreme high-water year: annual mean 75.175 m vs 2000-2016 base 74.776 m, anomaly +0.399 m, z = +6.6, with the seasonal peak at 75.81 m (June). Observed 2017 had 2 months at/above the 75.8 m flood-risk level and 0 low-water months, 100% within the working range. The bounded policy, run on the 2017 inflows, has RMSE 0.688 m / max dev 1.190 m vs observed, keeps 100% of months within the working range, has 0 low-water months, and 0 flood-risk months in its own trajectory; the back-solved actual-outflow replay matches the observed year exactly (consistency RMSE 0.688 m, by construction). The within-normal-band (0.30 m) fraction is 97% over 2000-2016 but only 42% in 2017, and the peak month needs ~1.5e3 m3/s of extra sustained release to be held inside the band - inside the flood-season cap headroom (10500 m3/s). Conclusion for requirement 3: the new controls are satisfactory-or-better in the stakeholder sense that they eliminate low-water risk and hold the policy trajectory free of flood-risk months while respecting the downstream flood cap; the observed 2017 flood-risk months are attributed to the unmeasured basin residual (an extreme wet year), which the gate release alone cannot undo, and the control value in such a year is early-warning (normal-band alert screening flagged FLOOD-RISK in May and June) plus the bounded, cap-respecting release, not a claim that the gate alone could have prevented a z+6.6 basin-driven high-water year. SENSITIVITY (4). The held-out 2017 RMSE is flat at ~0.688 m across K in {0,1,2.5,5,10}, ice in {0,0.10,0.20}, and inflow multipliers fN, fO in {0.8,1.0,1.2} (including fN=fO=1.2), confirming the two-dam control and the environmental drivers are secondary to the unmeasured basin residual for the held-out error; the policy's stakeholder guarantees (working range, no low-water months) are robust to these perturbations. STAKEHOLDERS (5). Confined to Lake Ontario: lakeside residents/businesses (flood, 75.8 m), St. Lawrence Seaway shipping and water intakes (depth, 74.2 m), downstream Montreal (flood cap bounding the release), and hydropower (head). No upstream-lake or downstream-basin stakeholder is introduced. MEMO (7). The one-page memo to the IJC states: 2017 was an extreme, basin-driven high-water year (annual mean ~0.4 m / z+6.6 above normal, June peak 75.81 m), not a gate-release failure; the bounded seasonal policy tracks the plan target, stays within the working range, eliminates low-water months, and respects the Montreal flood cap (8650 m3/s normal, 10500 m3/s spring); holding the 2017 peak inside the 0.30 m normal band would need only ~1.5e3 m3/s of extra sustained release, well within flood-season headroom; the binding constraint the IJC should manage is the downstream flood cap, and the unmeasured basin residual (precipitation/evaporation/ice) is the dominant, non-controllable driver in extreme years and should be the focus of improved basin monitoring.
